title: How do you build a training matrix for a clinical laboratory?
description: Build a clinical laboratory training matrix: CLIA competency for each test, biosafety, bloodborne pathogens, chemicals, specimen shipping and privacy duties.
shortAnswer: A clinical laboratory training matrix lists each testing and support role against every test system the person performs and every safety, transport and privacy rule that applies, then records the competency procedure, assessor, clock and evidence for each cell. In the United States the core is CLIA's six competency procedures for nonwaived testing, layered with biosafety, bloodborne pathogens, hazard communication, hazardous materials shipping and HIPAA duties.
keyTakeaways: CLIA competency is assessed per test, not per person: each nonwaived test a person performs needs all six procedures, semiannually in the first year and then at least annually.
A method or instrument change is a hard trigger: CLIA requires reevaluation before the person reports patient results on the new method.
Training is not competency: CMS states that training, performance appraisals and proficiency testing alone do not satisfy the documented competency assessment requirement.
Safety and shipping rows run on separate clocks: annual bloodborne pathogens training, recurrent hazmat training at least every three years, and air dangerous goods training within 24 months.
Retention periods differ by record: 2 years for most CLIA records, 3 years for bloodborne pathogens training records and select agent records, and 6 years for HIPAA documentation.

sections.heading: Why is a laboratory matrix organized by test system?

blocks.text: Because the central laboratory rule assigns competency to each test a person performs, a laboratory matrix needs a test system axis as well as a role axis. Under 42 CFR 493.1413(b)(8) for moderate complexity testing and 493.1451(b)(8) for high complexity testing, the six competency procedures apply to every test, so a technologist rotating across chemistry, hematology and microbiology carries a separate set of cells for each analyzer or method.

The general approach in [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) still holds, with three laboratory adjustments. Rows are people grouped by CLIA personnel role; a second dimension lists test systems; and safety, transport and privacy columns sit alongside, each with its own clock. Laboratories that also run nonclinical studies or manufacture medicines answer to different rules, which the [pharmaceutical site matrix guide](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-pharmaceutical-site) covers.

sections.heading: Which laboratory roles should form the rows?

blocks.text: Use the personnel roles named in the laboratory regulations, then add the support roles that safety and transport rules reach. CLIA names who may assess competency, so the assessor roles need their own rows.

sections.heading: Which laboratory obligations apply in each market?

blocks.text: Most laboratory regulation pages in this library are US federal, with international air transport rules and one EU directive. Each summary below draws only on the linked page.

items: **United States: test competency.** 42 CFR 493.1235 requires written policies to assess employee and, where applicable, consultant competency. The six procedures are direct observation, monitoring result recording and reporting, records review, observation of instrument maintenance, testing previously analyzed or blind samples, and problem solving ([CLIA competency](/regulations/clia-laboratory-personnel-competency-requirements)). CMS guidance revised in May 2025 says only people qualified as a technical consultant, technical supervisor or general supervisor may assess testing personnel.

**United States: accreditation.** Joint Commission's waived testing goal requires staff to be trained for each test with training documented, and competence assessed at orientation and annually using more than one method; its standards FAQ says a self-assessment checklist alone is not competency assessment ([Joint Commission competency](/regulations/joint-commission-staff-competency-requirements)).

**United States: biosafety.** The BMBL, a code of practice from CDC and NIH, expects supervisors to train staff on duties, hazards and precautions, keep records and provide annual updates; at BSL-2 and BSL-3 personnel demonstrate proficiency. Entities registered for select agents must train on biocontainment, biosafety, security and incident response under 42 CFR 73.15 ([laboratory biosafety](/regulations/biosafety-training-requirements-laboratories)).

**United States: worker safety.** 29 CFR 1910.1030(g)(2) requires training at initial assignment and at least annually for each employee with occupational exposure, during working hours and at no cost, including an interactive question and answer element ([bloodborne pathogens](/regulations/osha-bloodborne-pathogens-training-requirements)). 29 CFR 1910.1200(h) requires hazard communication training at initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced ([hazard communication](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements)).

**United States: transport and privacy.** Hazmat employees need initial training within 90 days of employment or job change and recurrent training at least every three years under 49 CFR 172.704 ([DOT hazmat](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training)). Where the laboratory is a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, 45 CFR 164.530(b) requires privacy training for new workforce members within a reasonable period and 164.308(a)(5) requires a security awareness program ([HIPAA](/regulations/hipaa-security-and-privacy-training)).

**International and Australia: air transport.** IATA DGR 1.5.1.2.1 requires the employer to ensure personnel are competent before performing dangerous goods functions, defined by function rather than job title. In Australia, CASA EX29/24 gives effect to two yearly training, with recurrent training within 24 months ([dangerous goods by air](/regulations/iata-dangerous-goods-training-requirements)).

**European Union.** Directive 98/24/EC Article 8(1) requires workers to receive training and information on precautions and actions for hazardous chemical agents, in a manner appropriate to the risk assessment and updated as circumstances change ([EU chemical agents](/regulations/eu-chemical-agents-directive-worker-training)).

sections.heading: How should a laboratory set and track the different clocks?

blocks.text: Record each clock as the rule states it, because laboratory rules use semiannual, annual, rolling 12 month, 24 month and three year intervals, plus event triggers. Rounding them to a single annual cycle overtrains some cells and misses others.

items: **First year CLIA cadence.** Competency is assessed at least semiannually during the first year a person tests patient specimens, then at least annually. A new hire therefore has two competency events in year one for every test system.

**Rolling annual intervals.** Bloodborne pathogens annual training must fall within one year of the previous training, so the due date moves with each completion rather than resetting each calendar year.

**Transport clocks.** DOT recurrent hazmat training is at least every three years; US air carrier hazmat training must be within the past 24 months, and CASA EX29/24 counts recurrent training within 24 months from the end of the month.

**Event triggers.** CLIA reevaluation on methodology or instrumentation change, hazard communication training when a new chemical hazard arrives, select agent refreshers on significant plan amendment, and HIPAA privacy training within a reasonable period of a material change.

**Rules with no interval.** Directive 98/24/EC asks for training updated for changing circumstances without fixing a cycle, so the laboratory sets one and documents why. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What evidence and retention should each laboratory row carry?

blocks.text: Each row should name the evidence type and the retention period, because laboratory inspectors look for competency evidence per test and the rules set different retention periods. Where one record serves several rows, keep it for the longest period that applies.

blocks.text: Content matters as much as retention. Select agent training records must include a means to verify understanding; DOT records need a certification of training and testing; and CMS says proficiency testing alone does not satisfy competency assessment. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers assembling these into an inspection file.

sections.heading: Which laboratory rules are changing as at November 2026?

blocks.text: Several proposals and transition deadlines touch laboratory rows, as recorded on the linked regulation pages. Track final rules as dated rows and proposals as watch items.

items: **November 20, 2026, United States:** employers must update hazard communication labeling, programs and training as necessary for substances under the 2024 Hazard Communication Standard revisions, with mixtures following by May 19, 2028.
**1 January 2027, international:** the 68th edition of the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations takes effect, so shipper training content should be checked against it.
**31 May 2027, Australia:** CASA EX29/24, which gives effect to the two yearly dangerous goods training requirement, is repealed at the end of that day unless replaced.

blocks.title: Proposed, not yet law
blocks.text: A CMS proposed rule published October 8, 2026 would rescind the separate competency procedures for provider-performed microscopy, without changing annual competency assessment for other nonwaived testing; comments close December 7, 2026. A draft NIH Biosafety Policy published September 14, 2026 would replace the NIH Guidelines when finalized. HHS proposed annual HIPAA security awareness training in January 2025, but no final rule had been found.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each laboratory obligation against its source clause, the test systems and roles it reaches, and the assessment point that shows competence, so the six CLIA procedures, biosafety proficiency and shipping certifications sit in one traceable structure. When a rule such as the provider-performed microscopy proposal is finalized, the affected cells are flagged. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Does every test a technologist performs need its own competency assessment?
faqs.a: Yes, for nonwaived testing. CMS states that the six procedures apply to every test a person performs, and all six must be documented each year. Laboratories often group tests on the same analyzer, but the record must still show the procedures for each test system the person runs.

faqs.q: Can a trainer who is not a supervisor sign off competency?
faqs.a: A trainer can sign off training, but CMS guidance says only people qualified as a technical consultant, technical supervisor or general supervisor may perform competency assessments of testing personnel. The director or technical supervisor may delegate evaluating and documenting competency to a general supervisor under 42 CFR 493.1463(b)(4).

faqs.q: Do waived testing staff need competency assessment?
faqs.a: CLIA does not require competency assessment for testing personnel in waived-only laboratories. Joint Commission's waived testing goal does, at orientation and annually, using more than one method, so accredited organizations should add those rows for staff running tests such as blood glucose or rapid strep.

faqs.q: Is proficiency testing enough to show competency?
faqs.a: No. Proficiency testing results can feed procedure five (testing previously analyzed or external samples) and records review, but CMS states that proficiency testing alone does not satisfy the competency assessment requirement. The other procedures, including direct observation and problem solving, still need their own evidence.
